--- title: "Tidying Data" icon: "file-slides" format: revealjs: scrollable: true execute: echo: true include-in-header: text: | --- ## Q&A > Is joining like [`xlookup`](https://support.microsoft.com/en-au/office/xlookup-function-b7fd680e-6d10-43e6-84f9-88eae8bf5929) or `vlookup` in Excel? Yes (though joining is more powerful) - `xlookup(*lookup_value*, *lookup_array*, *return_array*)` searches for `lookup_value` in `lookup_array` and returns the corresponding value from `return_array`. - *lookup_value* is the *key* - Exercise for experienced Excel users: think about what kind of join would this be. ::: notes `xlookup` is a left join, basically, assuming that the lookup array is unique. ::: ## Q&A > Where do "left" and "right" come from? ```python pd.merge(a, b, how='left')` # ^ ^ # left right ``` same as `pd.merge(b, a, how='right')` # Tidy data ## Tidy data > Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way. > > Leo Tolstoy . . . ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Characteristics of tidy data:** - Each variable forms a column. - Each observation forms a row. - Each type of observational unit forms a table. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Characteristics of untidy data:** - Varies. ::: ::: ## Data: Sales Let's construct two dataframes for fake sales data. (Here's two ways to make a dataframe by hand.) ::: {#24a866e5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # columns format customers = pd.DataFrame({ 'customer_id': [1, 2], 'item_1': ['bread', 'milk'], 'item_2': ['milk', 'toilet paper'], 'item_3': ['banana', None] }) # records format prices = pd.DataFrame( [ ['avocado', 5], ['banana', 0.57], ['bread', 3], ['milk', 2.5], ['toilet paper', 10], ], columns=['item', 'price'] ) ``` ::: ## Data: Sales ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} We have... ::: {#6a104eb0 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=129} ```{=html}
customer_id item_1 item_2 item_3
0 1 bread milk banana
1 2 milk toilet paper None
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} We want... ::: {#209a194b .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=130} ```{=html}
customer_id item_num item_name
0 1 item_1 bread
1 2 item_1 milk
2 1 item_2 milk
3 2 item_2 toilet paper
4 1 item_3 banana
5 2 item_3 None
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## `melt` the data ![](img/tidyr-longer-wider.gif) ::: aside Source: https://github.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain ::: --- ## Wider vs. longer ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **wider**: more columns ::: {#cd604b0c .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=131} ```{=html}
customer_id item_1 item_2 item_3
0 1 bread milk banana
1 2 milk toilet paper None
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **longer**: more rows ::: {#16f3d1ec .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=132} ```{=html}
customer_id item_num item_name
0 1 item_1 bread
1 2 item_1 milk
2 1 item_2 milk
3 2 item_2 toilet paper
4 1 item_3 banana
5 2 item_3 None
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Wide to Long: `melt` ::: {#234706db .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} customers ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=133} ```{=html}
customer_id item_1 item_2 item_3
0 1 bread milk banana
1 2 milk toilet paper None
``` ::: ::: ## Wide to Long: `melt` ::: {#6e65fcd3 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} customers.melt() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=134} ```{=html}
variable value
0 customer_id 1
1 customer_id 2
2 item_1 bread
3 item_1 milk
4 item_2 milk
5 item_2 toilet paper
6 item_3 banana
7 item_3 None
``` ::: ::: ## Wide to Long: `melt` - `id_vars`: primary key (columns that uniquely identify each row) - **not** transformed (but duplicated as needed) - a list, since a key can be multiple columns ::: {#40f49fa7 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} customers.melt( id_vars=['customer_id'], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=135} ```{=html}
customer_id variable value
0 1 item_1 bread
1 2 item_1 milk
2 1 item_2 milk
3 2 item_2 toilet paper
4 1 item_3 banana
5 2 item_3 None
``` ::: ::: ## Wide to Long: `melt` - `id_vars`: primary key - `var_name`: name of the column where *names* of columns are stored ::: {#3d9a2d90 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} customers.melt( id_vars=['customer_id'], var_name='item_num' ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=136} ```{=html}
customer_id item_num value
0 1 item_1 bread
1 2 item_1 milk
2 1 item_2 milk
3 2 item_2 toilet paper
4 1 item_3 banana
5 2 item_3 None
``` ::: ::: ## Wide to Long: `melt` - `id_vars`: primary key - `var_name`: new name for *variables* column - `value_name`: new name for *values* column ::: {#e76a7e3e .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} purchases = customers.melt( id_vars=['customer_id'], var_name='item_num', value_name='item' ) purchases ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=137} ```{=html}
customer_id item_num item
0 1 item_1 bread
1 2 item_1 milk
2 1 item_2 milk
3 2 item_2 toilet paper
4 1 item_3 banana
5 2 item_3 None
``` ::: ::: ## Why pivot? Most likely, because the next step of your analysis needs it . . . ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#f9b5d0e6 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} prices ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=138} ```{=html}
item price
0 avocado 5.00
1 banana 0.57
2 bread 3.00
3 milk 2.50
4 toilet paper 10.00
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#fc3344e1 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} purchases.merge(prices, how='left') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=139} ```{=html}
customer_id item_num item price
0 1 item_1 bread 3.00
1 2 item_1 milk 2.50
2 1 item_2 milk 2.50
3 2 item_2 toilet paper 10.00
4 1 item_3 banana 0.57
5 2 item_3 None NaN
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Long to Wide Sometimes helpful for analysis. Mostly helpful for reports. ::: {#01a89893 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} purchases.pivot( index='customer_id', columns='item_num', values='item' ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=140} ```{=html}
item_num item_1 item_2 item_3
customer_id
1 bread milk banana
2 milk toilet paper None
``` ::: ::: **Aside**: what if there are multiple values that would go in each box? `pivot` doesn't handle this cleanly. A related function, `pivot_table`, makes us explicitly specify what to do. For example, take the first one: ::: {#1f16aedd .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} purchases.pivot_table( index=['customer_id'], columns='item_num', values='item', aggfunc='first' ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=141} ```{=html}
item_num item_1 item_2 item_3
customer_id
1 bread milk banana
2 milk toilet paper NaN
``` ::: :::
